parts: Look at the last thing you bought. Check the price.
There is a good chance it ended in nine.
One study of advertisements, published in nineteen ninety-seven, found that about six in ten prices ended in nine.
You know the trick. Nine ninety-nine is really ten.
So why does it still work on us?
Here is the short answer. Your brain reads a price from left to right.
And it grabs the first digit before it looks at the rest.
So two ninety-nine feels like two-something, and three dollars feels like three. One cent apart, two different levels.
Researchers call this the left-digit effect.
And here is the key detail. It only shows up when the first digit changes.
Two ninety-nine against three dollars works. But two ninety against two ninety-nine does not, because the first digit stays the same.
But does it really change what people buy?
In three field experiments, two researchers changed the price endings on real products.
A nine ending raised demand in all three.
In one catalog test, the researchers wrote, a dress sold about a third better at thirty-nine dollars than at thirty-four.
It even works on numbers that are not prices.
In a study of more than twenty-two million used cars sold at auction, cars just under eighty thousand miles sold for about two hundred and ten dollars more than cars just over.
Now, the story you have probably heard is about cash registers.
According to the story, round prices let a cashier slip a bill into a pocket without opening the till.
A price like ninety-nine cents forces them to open it, to give change, and that announces the sale.
It is a nice story, and some writers repeat it. But it is not a proven explanation.
The real origin is murky. One writer guessed it began with a Chicago newspaper in eighteen seventy-five. Another argued that nine endings were still rare until the eighteen-eighties.
A Czech businessman, Tomas Bata, began using it widely in nineteen twenty. In Czechoslovakia, people called it Bata's price.
So how could you use this? Imagine you run a small shop.
First, price just under a round number, because that is where the first digit changes.
Second, use it where people shop by price: everyday items, and new products.
But for luxury, services, or anything where quality matters, nine endings can backfire. A clean round price can look more upscale.
And be careful with loud sale signs. The researchers saw some evidence that nine endings work less well next to them.
Subscriptions use it too. Nine ninety-nine a month sounds like nine.
Now the other side of the counter. How do you defend yourself?
Trick one: round every price up in your head. Nine ninety-nine is ten. Nineteen ninety-nine is twenty.
Trick two: for a monthly fee, multiply by twelve before you say yes.
Trick three: look at the small print. In the European Union, a shop generally has to show the price per kilo or per liter next to the price on the label.
Trick four: decide what the thing is worth to you before you look at the tag.
So the trick is simple. A price just under a round number reads as a lower level.
It seems to work best when shoppers know little about the product, and it works worse when quality is what matters.
One digit can nudge what we buy. And plenty of other numbers we never question have a stranger story.
Take the most famous number in running. Why is a marathon twenty-six point two miles?
